subtype: Stage 1: Work stress and quiet distance [Receiver]
passage: I'm Rajni, and I stayed with my sister Jasleen and her husband Harman for a week in Gurugram. Every evening was the same. Harman came in around nine, loosened his tie, said "hi" to both of us, and sat on the sofa with the TV on mute and his eyes half closed. He didn't seem angry, just emptied out. Jasleen would tell him something about her day, a funny thing her boss said, a plan for Sunday. He'd say "hmm" or "nice". By Thursday she had stopped telling. I found her in the kitchen, washing the same plate twice. "He doesn't need me here," she said. "I could be a lamp." I don't think Harman knew any of this. I'm not sure I did either, until then.

qa.q: What time did Harman usually come in?
qa.a: Harman came in around nine.

qa.q: What does Jasleen's remark "I could be a lamp" reveal?
qa.a: It reveals she feels invisible and unwanted, reading Harman's flat evenings as proof that her presence no longer matters.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this early stage?
qa.a: Jasleen could tell Harman how the quiet evenings feel to her, and Harman could explain he is drained, not uninterested, and offer a small time to connect.

qa.q: How does Harman seem to experience these evenings?
qa.a: He seems simply drained after work, not angry, and likely has no idea his quiet feels like rejection to Jasleen.

grounding: Shows a husband's exhausted, quiet evenings after work being read by his wife as a sign that she no longer matters.

passage:
Monday: Arnab came home from the hospital IT desk at ten, ate standing up, and fell asleep with his phone on his chest. Gopika covered him with a sheet and told herself it was just a bad week.
Thursday: She'd made his favourite fish curry. He ate it, said "good", and went to sit on the balcony in the dark. She washed up alone, wondering when she had turned into furniture.
The next Tuesday: Gopika didn't cook. She didn't wait up either. When Arnab came in and asked, "Where's dinner?", she said, "Didn't think you'd notice." He looked confused, almost hurt. He had only wanted quiet. He hadn't known she was counting the empty evenings.

qa.q: What did Gopika make on Thursday?
qa.a: She made his favourite fish curry.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling as she washed up alone?
qa.a: She felt invisible, wondering when she had turned into furniture.

qa.q: What could each of them do at this stage to stop the distance growing?
qa.a: Gopika could say "I miss you in the evenings" before resentment sets in, and Arnab could name his tiredness and offer a small window of time.

qa.q: How does Arnab experience the "Didn't think you'd notice" reply?
qa.a: He is confused and almost hurt, because he only wanted quiet and never meant to reject her.

grounding: Shows a worn-out husband wanting only quiet and his wife reading the empty evenings as proof she no longer matters.

Janak came home from the sugar mill after ten every night that harvest season. Simran would keep the rotis warm in the cloth, and the kerosene lamp lit, because the power always failed by nine in their kasba.
He'd eat, say "good," and lie down on the charpai in the courtyard. Eyes closed. No questions about her day, the goat that had fallen sick, the letter from her sister.
Simran sat by the lamp, folding and refolding the same cloth. Two years married, and already she felt like part of the furniture.
Janak didn't mean anything by it. His hands still smelled of cane and machine oil, and his body hummed with tiredness. But Simran couldn't see inside his tiredness.

qa.q: Why did Simran keep the kerosene lamp lit?
qa.a: Because the power always failed by nine in their kasba.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling as she folded and refolded the cloth?
qa.a: She felt lonely and unseen, as if she had become part of the furniture after only two years of marriage.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this stage?
qa.a: Simran could gently tell Janak she misses hearing from him, or he could share one line about his day, before the silence turns into a story that she doesn't matter.

qa.q: What is Janak experiencing when he lies on the charpai?
qa.a: He is exhausted from the mill and wants only quiet; he doesn't mean to reject Simran, but doesn't see how his silence feels to her.

grounding: A young wife reads her exhausted husband's quiet evenings during harvest as a sign she no longer matters, though he means no rejection.

passage:
Chidi's keys hit the bowl at half past eight. In their small flat in Manchester, Bisi was sitting at the kitchen table with two plates and a candle she'd bought on the way home.
"Hey," he said, and kissed the top of her head. Then he took his plate to the sofa and put on a football match with the sound low.
Bisi blew out the candle.
He'd been working double shifts at the hospital for three weeks, covering for a colleague. He came home grey in the face, asleep by ten.
She knew all that. Still, watching the back of his head, she wondered when she had stopped being worth looking at.

qa.q: How long had Chidi been working double shifts?
qa.a: For three weeks, covering for a colleague.

qa.q: What was Bisi feeling when she blew out the candle?
qa.a: She felt hurt and unimportant, wondering when she had stopped being worth looking at.

qa.q: What small step could help at this early stage?
qa.a: Bisi could tell Chidi she misses him and ask for ten minutes at the table, or Chidi could say he's exhausted but glad to see her, so the quiet isn't read as rejection.

qa.q: What is Chidi likely experiencing when he takes his plate to the sofa?
qa.a: He is drained after weeks of double shifts and wants quiet; he probably doesn't notice the candle or mean any rejection.

grounding: A young woman reads her exhausted partner's quiet evening as a sign she no longer matters, though his distance comes from work strain.

passage:
The hospital canteen was nearly empty at 10 p.m. when Ishita found Vijay at the corner table, still in his scrubs after a fourteen-hour shift.

"I brought you a dosa," she said, sitting across from him. "Guess what happened at my office today—"

"Mm." He nodded, eyes on his tea.

She tried again. "My manager finally said yes to the Pune trip."

"That's good." He rubbed his forehead. He hadn't looked up.

Ishita put down her fork. This was the fourth evening like this. In her head, a small voice said: He doesn't even want me here anymore.

Vijay, for his part, was thinking only that his ears were ringing from the ward and that silence felt like the kindest thing in the world. He had no idea she was reading his quiet as a verdict on her.

qa.q: How long was Vijay's shift?
qa.a: His shift was fourteen hours.

qa.q: What is Ishita worried about as she puts down her fork?
qa.a: She is hurt and worried that Vijay no longer wants her around, reading his flat evenings as rejection.

qa.q: What could each of them try to avoid this misunderstanding?
qa.a: Vijay could say, 'I'm wiped out, it's not you, I just need quiet,' and Ishita could ask directly instead of guessing.

qa.q: How does Vijay experience the evening differently from Ishita?
qa.a: Vijay simply feels exhausted and craves silence, with no intention of rejecting her and no idea how she reads it.

grounding: A worn-out partner wants only quiet after a demanding job, and the other reads the flat evenings as a sign she no longer matters.
